content: Chlamydia trachomatis is a bacterial pathogen responsible for the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI) worldwide. It causes significant morbidity and economic burden globally. The infection is most prevalent among young, sexually active adults. In women, it often leads to cervicitis, while in men, it causes urethritis. Additionally, it can result in extra-genital infections, such as rectal and oropharyngeal infections. Many cases are asymptomatic in both men and women, which can delay diagnosis and treatment. If left untreated, chlamydial infections can lead to severe complications, particularly in young women. These complications include ectopic pregnancy, salpingitis, and infertility due to damage to the upper reproductive tract. A more invasive serovar of Chlamydia trachomatis causes lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), which is increasingly observed among men who have sex with men (MSM) in certain settings. Maternal chlamydial infection is associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, such as preterm birth, low birth weight, conjunctivitis, nasopharyngeal infection, and pneumonia. Diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis can be achieved through various methods, including culture, direct immunofluorescence assays (DFAs), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs). However, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are preferred due to their superior sensitivity and specificity. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed updated guidelines for the treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis infections. These guidelines are based on the latest evidence and aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of chlamydial infections. The guidelines also support countries in updating their national treatment protocols. Key Recommendations for Treatment: 1. Uncomplicated Genital Chlamydia: Preferred treatments include: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Alternative options include: Tetracycline 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days. Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days. Ofloxacin 300 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. The choice of treatment may depend on factors such as cost, availability, and patient convenience. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnant women. 2. Anorectal Chlamydial Infection: Recommended treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose is an alternative, though less effective for anorectal infections. Doxycycline should not be used in pregnant women. 3. Genital Chlamydia in Pregnant Women: Azithromycin is recommended over erythromycin or amoxicillin due to better tolerability and fewer side effects. Dosages: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days. Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days. 4. Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV): Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days is the preferred treatment. Azithromycin 1 g orally weekly for 3 weeks is an alternative. Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days may be used if other options are unavailable. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnant women. 5. Ophthalmia Neonatorum (Chlamydial Conjunctivitis in Neonates): Azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day orally in a single daily dose for 3 days is recommended. Erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day orally in four divided doses for 14 days is an alternative. Azithromycin is preferred due to the risk of pyloric stenosis associated with erythromycin in neonates. Side effects should be monitored with either medication. Rationale for the Guidelines: The updated guidelines reflect changes in the epidemiology of STIs and advancements in diagnostic and treatment methods. They aim to provide clear, evidence-based recommendations to improve the management of chlamydial infections and reduce associated complications. Objectives: To provide evidence-based guidance on the treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis infections. To assist countries in updating their national guidelines for managing chlamydial infections. Methodology: The guidelines were developed by an international group of STI experts, clinicians, researchers, and program managers. Systematic reviews of treatment effectiveness were conducted, and the evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO protocols. These recommendations aim to improve patient outcomes, reduce the burden of chlamydial infections, and support global efforts to combat STIs effectively.
